turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. I'm Dr. Shah. What's been going on with this little guy?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This is Noah, he's four, and I'm his mom. He's had a fever and this cough, and I'm kind of freaking out, is he going to be okay?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Ruth, I live with them and I watch him. The fever's been longer than she's saying, just so you hear it from me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It has not. It started two days ago, Tuesday night, I remember because I was late getting home from work.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days? Honey, he was warm on Sunday. That's four days. I had my hand on his forehead before church.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right, so you two are landing in different places, somewhere in that two-to-four-day stretch for the fever. What about the cough?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cough I'm sure about. Three days. It gets worse when he lies down at night.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes, the cough is three days. I won't argue that one. It's the fever we don't agree on.
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): Throat hurt. I sick?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, he keeps grabbing his throat. And he's wiped out, he just wants to be held. Is being this tired normal, could it be pneumonia, should I have come yesterday?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get to all of that, I promise. How high has the temperature actually been at home?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I got 102 on our thermometer last night. One hundred and two.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That thermometer runs low. Mine said 103.8 before bed. He was burning up.
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Your thermometer is ancient, Ruth. It was 102.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, we won't settle the home number, I'll check him here. What have you given him for it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol. The children's Tylenol, the grape one. I gave two teaspoons, so that's 10 mils, last night and again this morning.

[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That is not what happened. I poured it, it was the little spoon, two and a half mils, and only last night. This morning I gave him ibuprofen instead, about a spoon, I think the 5 mil one, maybe.
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The ibuprofen, um, mm, I suppose, I wasn't home this morning. But the Tylenol was not two and a half, well, actually I watched him drink it last night.

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the acetaminophen dose is not something you two agree on, and the ibuprofen amount is basically a guess. I'm not going to pretend I know how many milligrams he already got.

[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While we're talking medicines, my sister swears by biotin for her hair, she takes it every morning. Not Noah. And his dad uses an inhaler, albuterol, because of his asthma.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dad's asthma I'll note as family history. The biotin and that inhaler are not Noah's. Any allergies for Noah himself?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No allergies. Nothing.

[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's not the whole story. He got spots all over after that pink antibiotic, the amoxicillin, when he was little. I can't even tell you if it was last spring or the winter before.
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pediatrician said that rash was viral, not a drug allergy. He does not have an amoxicillin allergy.
[SEG0025] person_4 (PATIENT): No spots.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm hearing a real disagreement there, so we'll decide on any antibiotic only after I look at him. Any vomiting or diarrhea with this?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No vomiting, and no diarrhea. Poops have been normal.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is he eating and drinking all right?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. He had some juice, I don't know.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any rash right now that you've actually seen on him?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. I thought I saw something in the bath and then it was gone.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been holding his tummy since yesterday and saying it hurts. That's been clear to me.
[SEG0033] person_4 (PATIENT): Tummy no.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): See, he's saying no. I never heard him complain about his stomach. Are belly bugs going around, is this appendicitis, kids get that right?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not jumping to appendicitis. One of you heard belly pain and he's denying it, so I'll press on his belly in a minute. Any trouble breathing, any wheeze?
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He's not wheezing, and he's not breathing hard. I watched him sleep.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgeries in the past? Asthma of his own, anything ongoing?
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No surgeries. No asthma. He's been a healthy kid, um, besides the usual colds.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Can I just say, the drive over was a nightmare. Forty minutes on the 101, and for what, a fender bender by the exit.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell me about it. And it's so hot out, like ninety-five, the car AC barely kept up.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Reminds me of that heat last August when we took the other grandkids to the lake. Jordan caught three fish. Three.
[SEG0042] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Jordan still talks about those fish. He wants a boat now. A boat, at eight years old.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, a boat. My nephew's the same with baseball. We sat through a whole little league game Saturday, and the ice cream after cost more than the snacks.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Little league concessions are a scam. Four dollars for a water. Next time I'm bringing a cooler, I swear.
[SEG0045] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We should've brought a cooler today, honestly. I left the good water bottles on the counter because we were rushing out the door.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the radio was all traffic, then that song Noah's dad hates, the one from the commercial. We changed the station twice.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a long morning before you even parked. Let me have a listen to you now, buddy.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Home?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soon. Ears first. Both eardrums look normal, no redness and no fluid behind them.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Throat's a bit red, nothing dramatic, no pus. Neck doesn't have any big swollen nodes.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lungs are clear all over, good air movement, no wheeze, no crackles. Belly is soft, no tenderness when I press, and he didn't guard.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vitals just now: temperature 100.4 Fahrenheit, heart rate 118, oxygen 98 percent, breathing 26 a minute. He looks all right between the coughs.
[SEG0053] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): 100.4 is lower than home. Is that bad that it dropped? Does he need a chest x-ray? Are you giving antibiotics? What if it's pneumonia and we miss it?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): My first thought walking in was, let's get a chest x-ray today and start amoxicillin. Fever plus cough in a four-year-old, I reach for that sometimes.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Amoxicillin? That's the one with the spots. I don't want that pink stuff again.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, and that's sitting here with what I just heard in his lungs. Scratch the x-ray for today. Scratch the antibiotic. I'm not prescribing amoxicillin, or any antibiotic.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is most likely a viral upper respiratory infection. I can't call that confirmed without a test, but it's my working read. His oxygen and those clear lungs argue against pneumonia.

[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no medicine at all? What do I do at 2 a.m. if he spikes, Tylenol or ibuprofen, how much is safe? Can he go to preschool tomorrow? What about his sister, she has a recital, wait, no, he doesn't have a sister, I'm spiraling.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Use the children's acetaminophen only. 160 milligrams, that's 5 milliliters of the usual suspension, by mouth, every six hours if the fever is bothering him. Don't give the ibuprofen on top of that today.
[SEG0060] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every six hours, 5 mils, okay. And if he won't take it, then what?

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If he won't take it, don't force a fight, just offer a cool drink and a light layer. Push fluids through the day. Come back sooner if he's working to breathe, if his lips look blue, or if he stops drinking.
[SEG0062] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the picture of the chest, that's just off the table?
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the fever is still going in three days, then we'll arrange a chest x-ray. Not today.
[SEG0064] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So we wait three days? What if I'm scared tomorrow? Is three days too long for a four-year-old, can I call somebody?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): If he's not better in three days, come back and see me. You can call the office sooner if your gut says he's worse, you don't have to sit on it.
[SEG0066] person_4 (PATIENT): Mommy, home.
[SEG0067] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, baby, almost. Doctor, the cough at night, humidifier or no? And honey, is honey okay, he's four?
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): A humidifier is fine if you already have one. A little honey is okay at his age, half a teaspoon, just to soothe the cough, not for the fever. No cough syrup.
[SEG0069] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll skip my sister's biotin advice. I know, I know.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do. Anything else that's actually about Noah before you head out?
[SEG0071] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think that's it. I'm still nervous, but I can do the 5 mils. Thank you for explaining it like that.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): You did fine bringing him in. We'll see how these next few days treat him.
[SEG0073] person_4 (PATIENT): Bye.

spec.situation: Parent brings a toddler or school-age child with fever and cough; the two parents (or parent and grandparent) disagree about how long, how high, and what was given (paracetamol vs ibuprofen, doses by 'spoon'). Child says only a few words.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Fever present and current, duration disputed 2-4 days; not certainly reported by family member alone.
